title: From a Programmed Cut to a Tested Knockout

scenes.tts: The first film showed that what you choose first sets what genetics can find. If Cas nine cuts the chosen gene, have you made a knockout?
scenes.narration: The first film showed that what you choose first sets what genetics can find. If Cas9 cuts the chosen gene, have you made a knockout?
scenes.caption: The first film showed that what you choose first sets what genetics can find. If Cas9 cuts the chosen gene, have you made a knockout?
scenes.visual: Continue the first film's 16:9 laboratory bench and exact colour map: PHENOTYPE or assay readout GREEN; chosen GENE PURPLE; GUIDE BLUE; Cas9 GOLD; PAM ORANGE; uncertain or mixed outcomes GREY. A PURPLE gene card from the gene-first lane expands into a large labelled DNA bar, not a molecular structure. A BLUE guide block and GOLD Cas9 block drift toward it. On the question, a GREEN 'function' meter appears at the far right with a question mark, while a moving arrow begins connecting target to function. Keep a small 'schematic' label at lower right.
The guide and Cas9 blocks continue drifting as the title 'From a Programmed Cut to a Tested Knockout' fades in for two seconds, then dissolves. The target-to-function arrow keeps growing behind it.

scenes.tts: A blue guide carries gold Cas nine to a matching purple gene region. A nearby orange P A M licenses binding and cleavage. Without a P A M beside it, a fully matching site is effectively ignored. With it, the complex makes a double-strand break at the chosen site.
scenes.narration: A blue guide carries gold Cas9 to a matching purple gene region. A nearby orange PAM licenses binding and cleavage. Without a PAM beside it, a fully matching site is effectively ignored. With it, the complex makes a double-strand break at the chosen site.
scenes.caption: A blue guide carries gold Cas9 to a matching purple gene region. A nearby orange PAM licenses binding and cleavage. Without a PAM beside it, a fully matching site is effectively ignored. With it, the complex makes a double-strand break at the chosen site.
scenes.visual: The PURPLE DNA bar fills most of the frame. A BLUE guide block slides along it, pauses over a matching labelled segment, and brings the GOLD Cas9 block with it. An ORANGE three-letter block labelled 'PAM' glows beside the match. A nearby grey segment lacking an orange block remains untouched and carries only a question mark. At the chosen site, the purple bar separates into two clean broken ends.

scenes.tts: The cut is only a handoff. One repair route rejoins ends without a supplied template. It may restore the sequence or leave an insertion or deletion. Another route copies a supplied template. One programmed site can therefore produce several repaired alleles. Their frequencies depend on local sequence and cell context.

scenes.visual: Carry the same broken PURPLE bar into a large branching repair track. Along the upper track, its ends slide together and transform successively into three labelled allele cards: 'restored', 'insertion', and 'deletion'. Along the lower track, a pale template card aligns beneath the break and a repaired purple card grows across it. The cards settle into a gently shuffling fan marked 'possible outcomes, schematic'; no probabilities appear.

scenes.tts: Follow an allele card through each checkpoint. Targeting means Cas nine reached the intended site. A cut means D N A broke. An edited allele carries a sequence change after repair. A functional knockout has lost gene function. These states require different evidence.
scenes.narration: Follow an allele card through each checkpoint. Targeting means Cas9 reached the intended site. A cut means DNA broke. An edited allele carries a sequence change after repair. A functional knockout has lost gene function. These states require different evidence.
scenes.caption: Follow an allele card through each checkpoint. Targeting means Cas9 reached the intended site. A cut means DNA broke. An edited allele carries a sequence change after repair. A functional knockout has lost gene function. These states require different evidence.
scenes.visual: The repair fan transforms into one horizontal pipeline filling the frame. Four large checkpoints appear in order: BLUE guide at 'targeted site'; separated PURPLE bar at 'cut'; changed PURPLE card at 'edited allele'; GREEN function meter at 'functional knockout?'. The first three checkpoints receive neutral evidence badges as named. The function meter keeps a question mark and never switches off merely because the earlier badges appeared.

scenes.tts: Now the dish contains several repaired allele cards. Some are unchanged, some shortened, and some lengthened. Must every cell in this dish have lost gene function? Look closely before you decide.
scenes.narration: Now the dish contains several repaired allele cards. Some are unchanged, some shortened, and some lengthened. Must every cell in this dish have lost gene function? Look closely before you decide.
scenes.caption: Now the dish contains several repaired allele cards. Some are unchanged, some shortened, and some lengthened. Must every cell in this dish have lost gene function? Look closely before you decide.
scenes.visual: The pipeline folds into a large culture dish containing a small set of cell cartoons. Above the dish, GREY, short PURPLE, and long PURPLE allele cards shuffle continuously. Each cell shows two face-down card slots to indicate a diploid pair, but their contents remain hidden. Large question text appears: 'Did every cell lose function?' No function meter changes.

Deliberate thinking pause. Hold 'Did every cell lose function?' The allele cards continue a slow shuffle above the dish; paired card slots inside the cells pulse faintly. No cards turn over and no answer appears.

scenes.tts: No. Cells can carry different pairs of alleles, because a diploid cell carries a pair. Some pairs contain an unchanged or in-frame allele. Others carry frameshifts in both copies. The dish is a mixed population, and an allele count is not a cell count.

scenes.visual: The question becomes 'mixed population'. Turn over two allele cards in each of four representative cells: unchanged plus shortened; in-frame plus shortened; two frameshift-labelled cards; and two different changed cards. Keep every cell's GREEN function meter as a question mark. A counter labelled 'alleles' separates visibly from another labelled 'cells'; no numerical values or proportions appear.

scenes.tts: Even frameshifts in both copies are still sequence predictions. A frameshift always shifts the reading frame downstream of the indel. Whether the protein's function is gone needs its own measurement. An in-frame change can retain partial function. Genotype narrows the claim; it does not finish it.

scenes.visual: Zoom to one cell with two frameshift-labelled PURPLE cards. A dotted arrow reaches a GREY protein-output box and stops at a question mark. Beside it, an in-frame card reaches a partly filled GREEN activity meter labelled 'possible partial function'. A third changed card reaches a differently sized GREY protein block marked 'unexpected product?'. All remain schematic possibilities, not asserted outcomes.

scenes.tts: Derive single-cell clones and identify both alleles separately. Look beyond a short amplicon when large changes could be missed. Measure the gene product or activity. Then ask whether the phenotype follows the genotype. Each step moves the claim forward.
scenes.narration: Derive single-cell clones and identify both alleles separately. Look beyond a short amplicon when large changes could be missed. Measure the gene product or activity. Then ask whether the phenotype follows the genotype. Each step moves the claim forward.

scenes.visual: One cell rises from the dish and divides into a uniform clone group. Two PURPLE allele cards turn face up beneath it. A short viewing window slides across each card, then expands into a longer window without claiming a result. Next, a GREY protein-output gauge and a GREEN phenotype meter animate side by side. A four-step arrow connects 'clone', 'genotype', 'product', and 'phenotype'.

scenes.tts: Use independent guides that alter the same gene at different sites. If they reproduce the phenotype, a guide-specific effect becomes less likely. Restore the gene in a way that resists the perturbation. If the phenotype reverses, the causal link becomes stronger. Still, no single control proves everything.

scenes.visual: Two BLUE guide blocks approach different sites on duplicate PURPLE gene bars. Their routes converge on matching GREEN phenotype-meter movements, so a GREY 'guide-specific?' tag shrinks but does not vanish. Then a resistant PURPLE gene card enters one cell; its green meter moves back toward the control state. Replace any check mark with 'stronger support', preserving uncertainty.

scenes.tts: Return to the pipeline. Cas nine can program a cut, but repair determines the allele. Sequencing can identify that allele, but function needs a phenotype or molecular readout. When genotype and phenotype agree across independent tests, the claim earns support.

scenes.visual: Rebuild the four-checkpoint pipeline from the same objects: BLUE guide and GOLD Cas9; broken PURPLE bar; repaired PURPLE allele card; GREEN phenotype and GREY molecular-readout meters. Evidence badges travel forward, then a bracket labelled 'agreement across tests' joins genotype and both readouts. The final badge reads 'supported claim', never 'proved'.

Clear everything to one centred line only: 'A genetic change supports function only when genotype and phenotype agree.' No title, logo, subtitle, or smaller line. A purple allele card and green phenotype glow move slowly toward alignment behind the words.
